opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the pressure has been very real, but I'd say it's a productive kind of pressure.

When ChatGPT came out, a lot of us in research had a moment of reflection. Many people in the community had been working on generative models for years, GANs, diffusion models, image synthesis, and suddenly the whole world was paying attention. The bar for what counts as an interesting result moved almost overnight. Before, you could write a nice paper with a clever idea trained on a modest dataset. After GPT, people started asking: does it scale? Does it generalize? Can it actually be useful to someone?

That changes how you work. Building large models is not just an algorithm problem anymore. It's a systems problem, a data problem, an infrastructure problem, and an organizational problem. You need data pipelines that can process enormous amounts of video or text, you need training stacks that run reliably on thousands of GPUs, and you need a team that can coordinate across all of those pieces. For someone with a traditional research background, that's a big shift. You go from thinking about your own experiment to thinking about how a hundred people's work fits together.

There's also pressure from the pace. Things move so fast that if you take six months to polish something, the landscape may have changed by the time you're ready. So you have to make bets earlier and with less certainty than you'd like.

For me, the way to handle it was to focus on a direction where I believed we could contribute something distinctive. Language models were already being pushed by many strong teams. What felt less explored was the physical world, models that understand how things move, interact, and change over time, which matters a lot for robotics, autonomous driving, and what people call physical AI. That gave us a clear mission, and a clear mission helps a lot with pressure, because you know what you're optimizing for.

So yes, it's intense. But I also feel lucky. This is probably the most exciting period in the field I've ever experienced, and the pressure comes from the fact that what we're building now really matters.

r001.rationale: The response describes pressure from shifting expectations, rapid pace, and the demands of building large models, but does not say mistakes revealed which practices mattered most.

r002.rationale: It does not identify spending resources on training without getting desired results as a source of psychological pressure.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, the pressure has been very real, and I think anyone working in this field who says otherwise is probably not being fully candid.

When ChatGPT came out, I remember the feeling very vividly. Many of us had been working on generative models for years, GANs, diffusion, image synthesis, video synthesis. We believed in the direction. But suddenly the whole world believed in it too, and overnight the expectations changed. Before, if you published a good paper and showed a nice demo, that was success. After, the question became: where is your model, how big is it, how does it compare, and why isn't it out yet?

For me the pressure came in a few layers. The first is scale. Training large models is not just a research problem anymore. It is an engineering problem, an infrastructure problem, a data problem, and frankly a money problem. You need thousands of GPUs, you need the pipelines to feed them, and you need a team that can keep a training run alive for weeks without wasting that compute. Every day a cluster sits idle or a run crashes, you feel it.

The second layer is speed. The field moves so fast that your plan from three months ago can look outdated. You have to decide: do we chase what others just released, or do we stay on our own path and trust that it pays off? That tension is constant. I try to remind the team that we cannot win by copying. We win by picking a direction where we have a real advantage and going deep.

The third layer is more personal. There is a feeling that if you are not working at the frontier, you are falling behind, and that affects how people sleep, how they treat their families, how they think about their careers. As a leader I have to manage my own anxiety so that it does not pour onto the team. If I panic, everyone panics.

What has helped me is focusing on what I actually believe matters. I have spent most of my career on visual generation, on simulation, on the physical world. Language models are incredible, but the world is not made of text. If you want AI that can drive a car, run a robot, or help a factory, it has to understand physics, space, time. That is a long-term bet, and having a long-term bet is what makes the short-term pressure bearable. You can look at the daily noise and say, this is not a distraction from our mission, this is just weather.

And one more thing I have learned: the pressure is also a privilege. Ten years ago we had to convince people that generative models were worth working on. Now nobody needs convincing. The resources, the talent, the attention are all here. So yes, it is stressful, but I would much rather carry this pressure than go back to a time when no one cared.

r001.rationale: The response describes pressure from infrastructure demands and rapidly changing expectations, but does not say that mistakes revealed which practices mattered most.

r002.rationale: It mentions the pressure of idle clusters and crashed runs wasting compute, but does not identify spending resources on training without desired results as invisible psychological pressure.

astra-6.text:
The pressure comes from how quickly the expectations change. You’re working toward one milestone, and before you reach it, the field has already moved. So there’s this constant question: are we being ambitious enough, and are we spending our time on the right problems?

With large models, that’s especially challenging because every experiment can require a lot of compute and engineering effort. You can’t test every idea. You have to make choices under uncertainty, and a disappointing result can be expensive.

But I think the way to handle that pressure is to stay focused on what you’re trying to learn. If you only react to the latest release, it becomes very difficult to build a coherent research direction. You need room for the team to experiment, understand failures, and do something that matters beyond the next benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response mentions costly experiments and disappointing results, but does not say mistakes revealed which practices mattered most.

sol-6.1.text:
The pressure has been quite intense. Since GPT’s rise, expectations have grown very quickly: people want more capable models, faster progress, and a clear sense of what comes next. But training a large model takes time, and the outcome of an experiment isn’t always predictable.

For me, the challenge is to stay focused under that pressure. You have to pay attention to what others are doing, while still asking: What problem are we trying to solve? What can we learn from this experiment? If every decision becomes a reaction to the latest release, it’s very difficult to do sustained research.
